claim: Physiological response to thermal stimuli in mammals is mediated by a structurally diverse class of ion channels.
source: Physiological response to thermal stimuli in mammals is mediated by a structurally diverse class of ion channels, many of which exhibit polymodal behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about mammalian thermal response that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Many temperature-sensitive ion channels in mammals exhibit polymodal behavior.
source: Physiological response to thermal stimuli in mammals is mediated by a structurally diverse class of ion channels, many of which exhibit polymodal behavior.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about temperature-sensitive ion channels.

claim: MthK channels are more efficient at rescuing K+ transport at 37°C than at 24°C.
source: Our functional complementation studies show that these channels are more efficient at rescuing K+ transport at 37°C than at 24°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional complementation assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Electrophysiological activity of purified MthK is extremely sensitive (Q10 >100) to heating particularly at low-calcium concentrations.
source: Electrophysiological activity of the purified MthK is extremely sensitive (Q10 >100) to heating particularly at low-calcium concentrations whereas channels lacking the calcium-sensing RCK domain are practically insensitive.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel electrophysiological recordings of purified MthK.

claim: MthK channels lacking the calcium-sensing RCK domain are practically insensitive to temperature.
source: Electrophysiological activity of the purified MthK is extremely sensitive (Q10 >100) to heating particularly at low-calcium concentrations whereas channels lacking the calcium-sensing RCK domain are practically insensitive.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data comparing MthK constructs with and without RCK domains.

claim: Temperature alters the coupling between the cytoplasmic RCK domains and the pore domain in MthK.
source: By analyzing single-channel activities at limiting calcium concentrations, we find that temperature alters the coupling between the cytoplasmic RCK domains and the pore domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel activity analysis at various calcium concentrations and temperatures.

claim: The Q10 is higher than 20 for a bonafide temperature-sensitive ion channel such as TRPV1 channel.
source: For instance, the Q10 (fold change in activity for a 10°C change in temperature) is higher than 20 for a bonafide temperature-sensitive ion channel such as TRPV1 channel compared to Q10 of 2–4 for most ion channels (Clapham and Miller, 2011; Islas and Qin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most ion channels have a Q10 of 2–4.
source: For instance, the Q10 (fold change in activity for a 10°C change in temperature) is higher than 20 for a bonafide temperature-sensitive ion channel such as TRPV1 channel compared to Q10 of 2–4 for most ion channels (Clapham and Miller, 2011; Islas and Qin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activity of TRPV1 is highly regulated by temperature.
source: In addition to TRPV1 (Caterina et al., 1997), the activity of TRPM8 (McKemy et al., 2002), TREK (Maingret et al., 2000), TMEM16A (Cho et al., 2012) and even prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Dib-Hajj et al., 2008) are all highly regulated by temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Caterina et al., 1997.

claim: The activity of TRPM8 is highly regulated by temperature.
source: In addition to TRPV1 (Caterina et al., 1997), the activity of TRPM8 (McKemy et al., 2002), TREK (Maingret et al., 2000), TMEM16A (Cho et al., 2012) and even prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Dib-Hajj et al., 2008) are all highly regulated by temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McKemy et al., 2002.

claim: The activity of TREK is highly regulated by temperature.
source: In addition to TRPV1 (Caterina et al., 1997), the activity of TRPM8 (McKemy et al., 2002), TREK (Maingret et al., 2000), TMEM16A (Cho et al., 2012) and even prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Dib-Hajj et al., 2008) are all highly regulated by temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maingret et al., 2000.

claim: The activity of TMEM16A is highly regulated by temperature.
source: In addition to TRPV1 (Caterina et al., 1997), the activity of TRPM8 (McKemy et al., 2002), TREK (Maingret et al., 2000), TMEM16A (Cho et al., 2012) and even prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Dib-Hajj et al., 2008) are all highly regulated by temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cho et al., 2012.

claim: The activity of prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels is highly regulated by temperature.
source: In addition to TRPV1 (Caterina et al., 1997), the activity of TRPM8 (McKemy et al., 2002), TREK (Maingret et al., 2000), TMEM16A (Cho et al., 2012) and even prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Dib-Hajj et al., 2008) are all highly regulated by temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dib-Hajj et al., 2008.

claim: Temperature-sensitive ion channels lack a common structural motif for sensing temperature.
source: As far as we know, these channels lack a common structural motif for sensing temperature, unlike their ligand activated counterparts.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field about the structural diversity of temperature-sensitive channels.

claim: Sensors of physical stimuli are not constrained by a specific domain in contrast to chemical sensors.
source: This lack of conserved structural module is not surprising given that sensors of physical stimuli are not constrained by a specific domain in contrast to chemical sensors (Kuriyan et al., 2012; Goldschen-Ohm and Chanda, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kuriyan et al., 2012 and Goldschen-Ohm and Chanda, 2017.

claim: MthK is an archaebacterial calcium-activated potassium channel from Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum.
source: In this study, we characterized the effect of temperature on gating of MthK, an archaebacterial calcium-activated potassium channel from Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum, a thermophile abundant in the hot springs of Yellowstone National park (Sandbeck and Ward, 1982; Jiang et al., 2002; Zeikus and Wolfe, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing MthK.

claim: Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum is a thermophile abundant in the hot springs of Yellowstone National park.
source: In this study, we characterized the effect of temperature on gating of MthK, an archaebacterial calcium-activated potassium channel from Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum, a thermophile abundant in the hot springs of Yellowstone National park (Sandbeck and Ward, 1982; Jiang et al., 2002; Zeikus and Wolfe, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sandbeck and Ward, 1982; Jiang et al., 2002; Zeikus and Wolfe, 1972.

claim: MthK is a tetramer with two transmembrane helices per subunit which come together to form a central pore.
source: MthK is a tetramer with two transmembrane helices per subunit which come together to form a central pore (Jiang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2002.

claim: The gating state of the central pore of MthK is regulated by RCK domains on the C-terminus of each subunit.
source: The gating state of the central pore is regulated by RCK domains on the C-terminus of each subunit which undergo a conformational change upon binding to calcium and other divalent cations (Smith et al., 2012; Pau et al., 2011; Dvir et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2012; Pau et al., 2011; Dvir et al., 2010.

claim: RCK domains undergo a conformational change upon binding to calcium and other divalent cations.
source: The gating state of the central pore is regulated by RCK domains on the C-terminus of each subunit which undergo a conformational change upon binding to calcium and other divalent cations (Smith et al., 2012; Pau et al., 2011; Dvir et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2012; Pau et al., 2011; Dvir et al., 2010.

claim: Parfenova and colleagues have previously suggested that temperature regulates the activity of MthK.
source: Parfenova and colleagues have previously suggested that temperature regulates the activity of MthK (Parfenova et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parfenova et al., 2006.

claim: The electrophysiological activity of MthK channels is highly sensitive to temperature in both native E. coli membranes and purified preparations.
source: Here, using an N-type inactivation-deficient variant of MthK (Kuo et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2020), we find that the electrophysiological activity of these channels is highly sensitive to temperature in both native E. coli membranes and purified preparations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The RCK domain is essential for temperature-dependent gating of MthK.
source: Our studies reveal that the RCK domain is essential for temperature-dependent gating and the primary effect of temperature is to alter the coupling strength between the calcium-sensing RCK domain and pore domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing constructs with and without RCK domains.

claim: The primary effect of temperature on MthK is to alter the coupling strength between the calcium-sensing RCK domain and pore domain.
source: Our studies reveal that the RCK domain is essential for temperature-dependent gating and the primary effect of temperature is to alter the coupling strength between the calcium-sensing RCK domain and pore domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by linkage analysis of single-channel data at different temperatures and calcium concentrations.

claim: Expression of functional potassium transporters or channels rescues the growth of LB2003 strain under low-potassium conditions.
source: Expression of functional potassium transporters or channels rescues the growth of this strain under low-potassium conditions (Parfenova et al., 2006; Hänelt et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parfenova et al., 2006 and Hänelt et al., 2010.

claim: Increased rescue of LB2003 strain can be directly correlated with a higher open probability of the expressed potassium channels.
source: Previous studies have shown that increased rescue of LB2003 strain can be directly correlated with a higher open probability of the expressed potassium channels (Cuello et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cuello et al., 2010b.

claim: MthK FL and MthK IR rescue the growth of LB2003 more efficiently at 36°C than at 18°C.
source: The expression of MthK FL and MthK IR rescues cell growth more efficiently at 36°C than at 18°C compared to empty vector controls or even expression of MthK ΔC.
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both MthK FL and MthK IR rescued the bacterial growth better at 37°C compared to 24°C.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, similar to the plate assay, both MthK FL and MthK IR rescued the bacterial growth better at 37°C compared to 24°C, consistent with a heat-activated phenotype of these channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by suspension culture assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MthK IR showed a more dramatic temperature-dependent complementation compared to MthK FL in suspension culture assay.
source: However, in the suspension culture assay, MthK IR showed a more dramatic temperature-dependent complementation compared to MthK FL, this could be a result of the lack of N-type inactivation in MthK IR construct.
evidence: This claim is supported by suspension culture assay data and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The cytosolic C-terminal domain of MthK is important for a robust temperature-dependent complementation.
source: These findings suggest that the cytosolic C-terminal domain of MthK is important for a robust temperature-dependent complementation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of complementation data between constructs with and without the C-terminal domain.

claim: MthK ΔC has a slightly increased survivability at 24°C compared to 37°C.
source: Surprisingly, we also find that MthK ΔC has a slightly increased survivability at 24°C compared to 37°C (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increased survivability of MthK ΔC at 24°C likely reflects better survivability of LB2003 at lower temperatures.
source: Similar temperature dependence is also observed in the presence of the blocker (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and therefore likely reflects better survivability of LB2003 at lower temperatures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the temperature dependence persists even with blocker present.

claim: Macroscopic currents of MthK IR increase at higher temperatures in the presence of 1.5 mM calcium.
source: Inside-out patch-clamp recordings in the presence of 1.5 mM calcium (close to the EC50 [Pau et al., 2010]) show that the macroscopic currents increase at higher temperatures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: At higher temperatures, especially at 41°C, robust MthK currents are observed after subtracting baseline leak.
source: Comparison of currents with and without barium shows very little baseline activity at low temperatures but at higher temperatures especially at 41°C, robust MthK currents are observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of currents with and without barium blocker.

claim: Temperature-sensitive activation is an intrinsic property of the MthK channel and does not require additional cellular cofactors.
source: Our findings also establish that temperature-sensitive activation is an intrinsic property of the channel and does not require additional cellular cofactors.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel recordings of purified and reconstituted MthK.

claim: The temperature dependence of the single-channel activity of purified MthK reconstituted in soybean lipids corresponds to a Q10 of over 100.
source: The observed temperature dependence of the single-channel activity of purified MthK reconstituted in soybean lipids corresponds to a Q10 of over 100, which is comparable to the canonical eukaryotic temperature-sensitive ion channels such as those of the TRP family of channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel activity measurements at different temperatures.

claim: The Q10 of over 100 for MthK is comparable to the canonical eukaryotic temperature-sensitive ion channels such as those of the TRP family.
source: The observed temperature dependence of the single-channel activity of purified MthK reconstituted in soybean lipids corresponds to a Q10 of over 100, which is comparable to the canonical eukaryotic temperature-sensitive ion channels such as those of the TRP family of channels.
evidence: This claim compares the measured Q10 of MthK to known values for TRP channels based on established knowledge.

claim: There is no significant change in the mean open-dwell time of MthK IR between 21°C and 37°C at 0.1 mM calcium.
source: There is no significant change in the mean open-dwell time between 21°C and 37°C (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of open-dwell times shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At 37°C, Po of MthK IR is about 20 times higher than those measured at lower temperatures at 0.1 mM calcium.
source: However, the open probability, Po, calculated from 5 min of continuous single-channel recordings, shows that at 37°C, Po is about 20 times higher than those measured at lower temperatures (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by open probability measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The mean close-dwell time of MthK IR changes from ~930 ms at 21°C to ~44 ms at 37°C at 0.1 mM calcium.
source: Thus, the high temperature profoundly shortens the residence times of the channel in the closed states which would dramatically reduce the stability of closed states and account for the change in Po.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the mean open time and Po values.

claim: High temperature profoundly shortens the residence times of MthK IR in the closed states.
source: Thus, the high temperature profoundly shortens the residence times of the channel in the closed states which would dramatically reduce the stability of closed states and account for the change in Po.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the calculated mean close-dwell times at different temperatures.

claim: The pore domain of the heat-sensitive TRPV1 channel when fused to the voltage-sensing domain of the Shaker potassium channel results in a chimeric channel with strong heat sensitivity.
source: Such a hypothesis would parallel a recent study which showed that the pore domain of the heat-sensitive TRPV1 channel when fused to the voltage-sensing domain of the prototypical Shaker potassium channel, results in a chimeric channel with strong heat sensitivity, suggesting that pore domain of TRPV1 might retain the essential structural elements for temperature sensitivity (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The pore domain of TRPV1 might retain the essential structural elements for temperature sensitivity.
source: Such a hypothesis would parallel a recent study which showed that the pore domain of the heat-sensitive TRPV1 channel when fused to the voltage-sensing domain of the prototypical Shaker potassium channel, results in a chimeric channel with strong heat sensitivity, suggesting that pore domain of TRPV1 might retain the essential structural elements for temperature sensitivity (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the cited study.

claim: The mean open-dwell time of MthK PO at 21°C corresponds to 19 ms.
source: The mean open-dwell time at 21°C corresponds to 19 ms, whereas at 37°C, it corresponds to 5 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single-channel recordings of MthK PO.

claim: The mean open-dwell time of MthK PO at 37°C corresponds to 5 ms.
source: The mean open-dwell time at 21°C corresponds to 19 ms, whereas at 37°C, it corresponds to 5 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single-channel recordings of MthK PO.

claim: The ~4-fold change in mean open-dwell time of MthK PO almost entirely accounts for 4.8-fold higher nPo near room temperature.
source: This ~4-fold change in mean open-dwell time of Mthk PO almost entirely accounts for 4.8-fold higher nPo near room temperature.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of open-dwell times and nPo values.

claim: Opening of the isolated pore domain of MthK is not temperature-sensitive.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that opening of the isolated pore domain of MthK is not temperature-sensitive and that structural elements from RCK domains are required for its exquisite heat-sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of temperature effects on MthK IR versus MthK PO.

claim: Structural elements from RCK domains are required for the exquisite heat-sensitivity of MthK.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that opening of the isolated pore domain of MthK is not temperature-sensitive and that structural elements from RCK domains are required for its exquisite heat-sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of temperature effects on constructs with and without RCK domains.

claim: TRPV1 channels exhibit hysteresis and irreversible loss of activity upon repeated stimulation.
source: Although the canonical heat-sensitive TRPV1 channels has been used to probe the thermodynamics of temperature-sensitivity, recent studies have shown that these channels exhibit hysteresis and irreversible loss of activity upon repeated stimulation (Sánchez-Moreno et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sánchez-Moreno et al., 2018.

claim: Persistent heat causes rapid desensitization of the wild-type TRPV1 channel.
source: Other studies have also shown that persistent heat causes rapid desensitization of the wild-type TRPV1 channel (Luo et al., 2019; Cui et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2019 and Cui et al., 2012.

claim: MthK IR does not show significant temperature-dependent desensitization when patches are held at high temperatures (39°C) up to 5 min.
source: For MthK IR, we have not observed any significant temperature-dependent desensitization when patches are held at high temperatures (39°C) up to 5 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by extended single-channel recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Po values of MthK IR at room temperature are similar to those obtained after heat activation.
source: Furthermore, the Po values of MthK IR at room temperature are similar to those obtained after heat activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) indicating that the temperature-dependent gating is reversible (between 21°C and 37°C) and that MthK IR may serve as a suitable model for further thermodynamic analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The temperature-dependent gating of MthK IR is reversible between 21°C and 37°C.
source: Furthermore, the Po values of MthK IR at room temperature are similar to those obtained after heat activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) indicating that the temperature-dependent gating is reversible (between 21°C and 37°C) and that MthK IR may serve as a suitable model for further thermodynamic analysis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of Po values before and after heat activation.

claim: The EC50 of calcium for MthK IR at 21°C is ~0.7 mM.
source: Our measured dose-response curves of MthK reveal that the EC50 of calcium at 21°C and 37°C are only modestly different (EC50 ~0.7 mM at 21°C versus 0.6 mM at 37°C), although there is a decrease in the steepness of the dose-response curve (4.0 at 21°C versus 1.8 at 37°C) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response curve analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The EC50 of calcium for MthK IR at 37°C is ~0.6 mM.
source: Our measured dose-response curves of MthK reveal that the EC50 of calcium at 21°C and 37°C are only modestly different (EC50 ~0.7 mM at 21°C versus 0.6 mM at 37°C), although there is a decrease in the steepness of the dose-response curve (4.0 at 21°C versus 1.8 at 37°C) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response curve analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Hill coefficient of the calcium dose-response curve for MthK IR is 4.0 at 21°C.
source: Our measured dose-response curves of MthK reveal that the EC50 of calcium at 21°C and 37°C are only modestly different (EC50 ~0.7 mM at 21°C versus 0.6 mM at 37°C), although there is a decrease in the steepness of the dose-response curve (4.0 at 21°C versus 1.8 at 37°C) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response curve analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Hill coefficient of the calcium dose-response curve for MthK IR is 1.8 at 37°C.
source: Our measured dose-response curves of MthK reveal that the EC50 of calcium at 21°C and 37°C are only modestly different (EC50 ~0.7 mM at 21°C versus 0.6 mM at 37°C), although there is a decrease in the steepness of the dose-response curve (4.0 at 21°C versus 1.8 at 37°C) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response curve analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Much higher temperature dependence of MthK activity was observed at the lowest concentrations of calcium.
source: Interestingly, much higher temperature dependence of MthK activity was observed at the lowest concentrations of calcium, where the RCK domains are primarily in apo state (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The apo-RCK domain regulates temperature-dependent pore gating.
source: However, given our observations that robust thermosensitivity of MthK requires intact RCK domains and low occupancy of calcium-binding sites, we conclude that the apo-RCK domain regulates temperature-dependent pore gating.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that temperature sensitivity is highest at low calcium concentrations.

claim: The apo-RCK domain must interact with the pore.
source: Our findings also imply that apo-RCK domain must interact with the pore, consistent with a recent allosteric model (Lewis and Lu, 2019) but in contrast to earlier simple models (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the findings and is consistent with a cited recent model.

claim: Going from 21°C to 37°C, Δχ changes from 4.5 to 2.2 for MthK IR.
source: Going from 21°C to 37°C, Δχ changes from 4.5 to 2.2, which corresponds to a change in coupling energy from 2.6 to 1.4 kcal/mol.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the Hill plot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The change in Δχ from 21°C to 37°C corresponds to a change in coupling energy from 2.6 to 1.4 kcal/mol.
source: Going from 21°C to 37°C, Δχ changes from 4.5 to 2.2, which corresponds to a change in coupling energy from 2.6 to 1.4 kcal/mol.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the Δχ values.

claim: The overall allosteric coupling is favorable at both 21°C and 37°C.
source: The change in Δχ indicates that while the overall allosteric coupling is favorable at both temperatures (i.e. the calcium-binding sites and the pore prefer to exist in 'like' conformations), the coupling interaction is much weaker at 37°C with respect to 21°C, which is also consistent with the relatively shallower dose response curve observed at 37°C.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the positive Δχ values at both temperatures.

claim: The coupling interaction is much weaker at 37°C with respect to 21°C.
source: The change in Δχ indicates that while the overall allosteric coupling is favorable at both temperatures (i.e. the calcium-binding sites and the pore prefer to exist in 'like' conformations), the coupling interaction is much weaker at 37°C with respect to 21°C, which is also consistent with the relatively shallower dose response curve observed at 37°C.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the change in Δχ values.

claim: Mammalian thermoTRPs are founding members of temperature-sensitive ion channels that respond exquisitely to thermal stimuli.
source: Mammalian thermoTRPs are founding members of temperature-sensitive ion channels that respond exquisitely to thermal stimuli (Caterina et al., 1997; McKemy et al., 2002; Peier et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caterina et al., 1997; McKemy et al., 2002; Peier et al., 2002.

claim: STIM1-Orai complex is activated by temperature.
source: But in addition to thermoTRPs, many other structurally dissimilar ion channels such as STIM1-Orai complex are also activated by temperature (Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xiao et al., 2011.

claim: Single channel inside out patch clamp recordings of purified reconstituted MthK show that they are extremely sensitive to temperature between 20°C and 40°C.
source: Single channel inside out patch clamp recordings of purified reconstituted MthK show that they are extremely sensitive to temperature between 20°C and 40°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel recording data.

claim: Over the range of 20°C to 40°C, the open probability of MthK IR increases about two orders of magnitude in low-calcium concentrations.
source: Over this range, the open probability of MthK IR increases about two orders of magnitude in low-calcium concentrations making it exquisitely sensitive to temperature, much like the prototypical eukaryotic thermosensors.
evidence: This claim is supported by open probability measurements at different temperatures.

claim: The region near the selectivity filter in the pore domain of TRPV1 contributes to temperature-sensitivity.
source: Studies on the TRPV1 which has been widely used as a model system to understand temperature-sensitivity shows that the region near the selectivity filter in the pore domain contributes to temperature-sensitivity (Zhang et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2018 and Kim et al., 2013.

claim: The region near the pore gates in TRPV3 channel is responsible for temperature dependence.
source: Structural studies on TRPV3 channel, another thermosensitive ion channel, suggest that the region near the pore gates is responsible for temperature dependence (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2019.

claim: At saturating calcium concentrations, the χ+ values of MthK IR are hardly affected by temperature in contrast to those at low calcium concentrations.
source: Our data clearly shows that at saturating calcium concentrations, the χ+ values are hardly affected by temperature in contrast to those at low calcium concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Hill plot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Increasing the temperature decreases the Po of MthK PO channel by four-fold.
source: Second, our single channel data of the MthK PO construct shows that increasing the temperature actually decreases the Po of the channel at high temperature by four-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel data of MthK PO shown in Figure 3.

claim: IPTG induction of the MthK ΔC construct rescues the growth of the LB2003 in low potassium at 28°C and 24°C.
source: Third, complementation plate assays at 28°C and 24°C clearly shows that the IPTG induction of the MthK ΔC construct rescues the growth of the LB2003 in low potassium (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The temperature-stability of C-terminal coiled-coil motif in the bacterial voltage-gated Na+ channel directly regulates the opening and closing of the pore domain.
source: Minor and colleagues have shown that the temperature-stability of C-terminal coiled-coil motif in the bacterial voltage-gated Na+ channel directly regulates the opening and closing of the pore domain (Arrigoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arrigoni et al., 2016.

claim: The coiled-coil motif in Hv1 channels regulates its temperature-dependent activity.
source: Similar studies on Hv1, a voltage-gated proton channel, shows that the coiled-coil motif in these channels also regulates its temperature-dependent activity (Takeshita et al., 2014; Fujiwara et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Takeshita et al., 2014 and Fujiwara et al., 2012.

claim: The temperature dependence of bacterial voltage-gated Na+ channels and Hv1 channels is much lower than that of a prototypical temperature-sensitive TRP channel.
source: Nevertheless, it should be pointed out that the temperature dependence of these channels is much lower than that of a prototypical temperature-sensitive TRP channel (Clapham and Miller, 2011) and for that matter, MthK as shown here.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with known Q10 values from literature and the measured Q10 of MthK.

claim: Recent X-ray and cryoEM structures of the full-length MthK show that the pore and RCK domains are not in physical contact except through the connecting linker.
source: Recent X-ray and cryoEM structures of the full-length MthK show that the pore and RCK domains are not in physical contact except through the connecting linker (Fan et al., 2020; Kopec et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fan et al., 2020 and Kopec et al., 2019.

claim: The linker between pore and RCK domains appears to be more ordered in the calcium free state than in the presence of calcium.
source: This linker appears to be more ordered in the calcium free state than in the presence of calcium (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fan et al., 2020.

claim: The structure of closed MthK channel shows that the linker latches onto the RCK domains via hydrophobic and possible salt bridge interactions.
source: The structure of closed MthK channel shows that the linker latches onto the RCK domains via hydrophobic and possible salt bridge interactions.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis from cited studies.

claim: Upon calcium binding, hydrophobic interactions between the linker and RCK domains may be disrupted causing the linker to become disordered.
source: Upon calcium binding, these hydrophobic interactions may be disrupted causing the linker to become disordered.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural observations.

claim: Elevated temperature may disrupt interactions between the linker and RCK domains in the apo state and thereby manipulate the pore opening.
source: Similarly, elevated temperature also may disrupt these interactions in the apo state and thereby manipulate the pore opening (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of temperature sensitivity.

claim: The linker may play a key role in coupling the apo-RCK domain to the conformation of the pore domain.
source: Thus, one would posit that the linker may play a key role in coupling the apo-RCK domain to the conformation of the pore domain.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural and functional observations.

claim: MthK is from Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum.
